title: The Stonewall Dutch
description: A reliable defense, focusing on building a brick wall of pawns on light squares. Features many attacking ideas, so good for more aggressive/tactical players rather than patient ones.

r1b1k2r/pp1n3p/2pqpnp1/3p1p2/2PP4/2NBPN2.text:
White might prepare that with Rc1, taking control of the c-file.

We'll simply bring the king to safety.

r1b1k2r/pp1nq1pp/2p1pn2/2Pp1p2/3P4/2NBPN.text:
If White castles...

Let's go for the ...g6-idea, enabling ...e5 again!

This is an important concept I want you to remember.

r1b1k2r/pp1nq1pp/2p1pn2/2PpNp2/3P4/2NBP3.text:
White could choose to play more aggressively and play Ne5 instead of castling here.

We won't let that knight stay on the active e5-square for long!

That's why we played ...Nd7, after all.

r1b1k2r/pp1nq2p/2p1pnp1/2Pp1p2/1P1P4/2NB.text:
White can't stop ...e5 now, but they can continue expanding on the queenside.

Let's create chaos in the center!

We are threatening ...e4 here...

r1b1k2r/pp1nq2p/2p2np1/2PpPp2/1P6/2NBPN2.text:
So it's probably best for White to capture in the center.

Naturally, we'll recapture with the knight.

r1b1k2r/pp2q1pp/2p1p3/2PpPp2/6n1/2NBP3/P.text:
And I recommend ...Ng4 here, with an attack on the e5-pawn.

White's c5-pawn is also hanging!

How are they going to defend their weaknesses?

Something like f4 hangs the e3-pawn as well.

r1b1k2r/pp2q2p/2p2np1/2PpNp2/1P6/2NBP3/P.text:
White will often trade here...

But that lets us centralize our queen with an attack on the knight on c3!

The queen in the center now also targets the h2-pawn, and we could use that to create a small attack.

r1b1k2r/pp5p/2p2np1/2Ppqp2/1P6/2NBP3/P1Q.text:
One of the lines is for White to activate the queen and defend the knight.

Let's attack the h2-pawn immediately!

r1b1k2r/pp5p/2p3p1/2Ppqp2/1P4n1/2NBP1P1/.text:
This forces White to play g3, weakening their light squares on the kingside.

And we've still got our light-squared bishop!

r1b2rk1/1p1n3p/2pq2p1/p2p1p2/1P1Pn3/P1NB.text:
Remember to challenge the b4-pawn right away!

Our position is comfortable, with the knight coming to f6 to support the knight on e4. The only problem is the bishop on c8.

On the other hand, White might play Qb3 to develop and instigate on the queenside.

r1b2rk1/pp1Nq1pp/2p1p3/3p4/2PPp3/2N1P3/P.text: So they would probably capture on d7.

r1b2rk1/pp1n3p/2pq1np1/3p1p2/3P4/P1NBPN2.text:
Not having made us recapture in the center with the c-pawn, one of the main plans for White is to expand on the queenside.

They are aiming for b4.

We'll get an extremely strong knight on the e4-square, though.

White can't capture with the knight as they would get forked!

r1b2rk1/pp1n3p/2pq2p1/3p1p2/1P1Pn3/P1NBP.text:
They could continue with b4, though.

Once they do...

r1b2rk1/pp1n3p/2pqpnp1/3P1p2/3P4/2NBPN2/.text:
Now it makes sense for White to capture in the center.

Capturing with the c-pawn would let White get a very active rook on c1, and access to the b5-square, 
so I recommend capturing with the e-pawn.

Now we won't be able to achieve the ...e5-push, but at least we've opened up the e-file and can shove the knight into the e4-square.

r1b2rk1/pp1nq1pp/2p1p3/2PpPp2/5Bn1/2NBP3.text:
Also, capturing with the d-pawn weakens the c5-pawn as well.

Now, we attack both the e5- and the c5-pawns!

White can't defend both.

r1b2rk1/pp1nq1pp/2p1pn2/2PpPp2/5B2/2NBP3.text:
That's why they'll probably recapture with the pawn.

But now their bishop on f4 is blocked in and basically useless.

r1b2rk1/pp1nq1pp/2pbpn2/2PpNp2/3P1B2/2NB.text:
If White tries c5 now, it's different, as our knight is already on d7.

In this instance, we can capture on e5.

If White captures with the bishop, we'll trade it for our knight on d7.

r1b2rk1/pp5p/2p3p1/2Ppqp2/1P4n1/2NBP1P1/.text:
Castling here gives us a comfortable position.

We've got a lot of space in the center and active pieces.

Next, we'll activate the light-squared bishop and connect the rooks.

r4rk1/pp1bq1pp/2p1p3/3p4/2PPp3/2N1P3/PP3.text:
And let's recapture.

Our course of action should be to make use of the open f-file and rotate our rooks to the h6- and f6-squares.

That way, we can attack the king!

r4rk1/pp1nq1pp/2p1b3/3pNp2/3PBP2/2N1P3/P.text: Should White choose to get rid of our dangerous knight in the center...

r4rk1/pp1nq1pp/2p1b3/4Np2/3PpP2/2N1P3/PP.text:
Now our light-squared bishop comes to life, which is always a good achievement in the Stonewall Dutch!

Our plan now is simple: get the rooks to the d- and the c-files, and play for ...c5!

Now that we captured ...dxe4, ...c5 is the key pawn break we want to achieve, breaking apart White's already shaky structure in the center.

rn3rk1/pp2q1pp/2p1b3/3pNp2/3PnP2/2NBP3/P.text:
Solidifying the knight on e5.

Now let's activate our own knight and challenge the knight on e5.

rnb1k2r/pp2q1pp/2p1pn2/2Pp1p2/3P4/2NBPN2.text:
A normal developing move by White, preparing castling.

White attacks the f5-pawn and prevents ...e5 for the moment, if we develop our queenside knight.

I recommend developing the knight here nevertheless and controlling that crucial e5-square.

rnb1k2r/pp4pp/2pqpn2/2Pp1p2/3P4/2N1PN2/P.text:
One of the approaches for White is to try and close down the center with tempo on our queen.

They want to play positionally and with space.

Retreating the queen to e7 is good, still keeping an eye on the e5-square.

Knowing we want to play ...e5, White might play Ne5 themselves first!

rnb1k2r/pp4pp/2pqpn2/3p1p2/2PP4/2NBPN2/P.text:
Another move you could face is Bd3, activating the bishop and putting pressure on the f5-pawn.

This doesn't allow us to play ...e5 immediately, as our f5-pawn would be loose, although defended.

That's why I recommend defending the f5-pawn here with ...g6.

Although it weakens the kingside, the prospects of ...Nbd7 and ...e5 are extremely powerful.

rnb1k2r/pp5p/2pqpnp1/3p1p2/2PP4/2NBPN2/P.text:
White would eventually castle.

We'd continue development and control the e5-square with one more piece.

Now pushing ...e5 is definitely on the cards, unless White captures in the center, as you'll see.

rnb1nrk1/ppb1q1pp/2p1p3/2PpNp2/3P1B2/2NB.text:
I recommend retreating to e8 and protecting the vulnerable bishop on c7.

Next, we'll develop the knight to d7 and try to trade on e5.

rnb2rk1/pp2q1pp/2p1p3/3p1p2/2PPn3/2NBPN2.text:
We'll recapture, and our position is stable. 

Our ideas include: ...Bd7-e8-h5, or playing ...Nd7 to counter White's knight jump into e5. 

We'll recapture on d5 with our e-pawn. 

Another option is a kingside attack with either rook lift or pawn storm.

rnb2rk1/pp2q1pp/2p1p3/3pN3/2PPp3/2N1P3/P.text:
If they place the knight in the center, you should know how to respond by now.

Activate your own knight and challenge White's!

White can't defend the knight with f4 here because we could capture en passant.

rnb2rk1/pp2q1pp/2p5/3pNp2/3Pn3/2NBP3/PP3.text:
If they shove the knight into the center, our main idea is ...Nd7.

In this instance, we can activate the light-squared bishop first.

rnb2rk1/pp2q1pp/2pbpn2/2PpNp2/3P1B2/2NBP.text:
Instead of castling, c5 is definitely more aggressive with an attack on the bishop.

However, it is pretty committal; White closes down the center.

The only logical move.

rnb2rk1/pp2q1pp/2pbpn2/3pNp2/2PP1B2/2NBP.text:
White castles...

And we'll do just that, challenging the knight on e5.

If White lets us capture, they'll destabilize their own center.

rnbq1rk1/pp2B1pp/2p1p3/3p1p2/2PPn3/2NBPN.text: This usually causes a trade of bishops, as White doesn't really have any other move here, unless they capture the knight on e4.

rnbq1rk1/pp2B1pp/2p1p3/3p4/2PPp3/2N1PN2/.text:
White basically has to capture on e7 now and attack our queen.

We'll take back, naturally.

rnbq1rk1/pp2B1pp/2p5/3p1p2/3Pn3/2NBPN2/P.text:
White captures...

And we'll capture back.

rnbq1rk1/pp2b1pp/2p1p3/3p1pB1/2PPB3/2N1P.text:
If White chooses to remove the knight immediately...

We'll recapture with the f-pawn.

This way a file for our rook opens up and we attack the knight on f3.

There is still the tension between the dark-squared bishops.

rnbq1rk1/pp2b1pp/2p1p3/3pN3/2PPp3/P3P1B1.text:
And we can simply retreat to e7.

What's left is the usual idea of ...Nd7 and trading on e5.

Later on, we'll figure out what to do with the light-squared bishop, but we definitely have a more comfortable position to play!

rnbq1rk1/pp2b1pp/2p1pn2/3p1pB1/2PP4/2NBP.text:
White brings the king to safety as well.

Now the knight is in the center of the board!

rnbq1rk1/pp2b1pp/2p2n2/3p1pB1/3P4/2NBPN2.text:
White could do the same.

Now that most of the pieces have been developed, what's the key move we want to play in the center?

Getting the knight to the great outpost.

rnbq1rk1/pp4pp/2p1p3/3pN3/1bPPp3/P3P1B1/.text: White will probably choose to kick out the bishop from the active b4-square.

rnbq1rk1/pp4pp/2pbpn2/3pNp2/2PP1B2/2NBP3.text:
They continue developing with Bd3, ready to castle.

We are a bit cramped, but we can still develop!

Next, we'll try to get the knight into the game and possibly trade on e5.

rnbqk2r/pp2b1pp/2p1pn2/3p1pB1/2PP4/2NBPN.text:
White continues developing too, ready to castle.

This line is very positional, with our key idea being to place the knight on the e4-square we control.

Let's castle first.

rnbqk2r/pp2b1pp/2p2n2/3p1pB1/3P4/2NBPN2/.text:
White activates their bishop to d3, with an attack on the f5-pawn.

Once we castle...

rnbqk2r/pp4pp/2p1p3/3pN3/1bPPp3/4P1B1/PP.text:
Now they are forced to move the king and block their own development.

They also lose castling rights!

On the other hand, we don't.

Our rook is extremely active now.

rnbqk2r/pp4pp/2pBpn2/3p1p2/2PP4/2N1PN2/P.text:
If they capture, at least we've gotten rid of their active bishop.

We'll recapture with the queen.

One of the main ideas for the near future would be to achieve the ...e5-push and grab even more space in the center, after completely controlling the e4-square.

rnbqk2r/pp4pp/2pbp3/3p1p2/2PPN3/4PNB1/PP.text:
That's why White often chooses to trade here.

Capturing with the f-pawn keeps our structure solid and protected.

We attack the knight, and if we castle in the future, we'll have the f-file for our rook.

rnbqk2r/pp4pp/2pbp3/3pN3/2PPp3/4P1B1/PP3.text:
White can still occupy the e5-square with their knight, though.

Can you see what diagonal has opened up for one of our pieces?

We'll give a check on the b4-square!

Remember, whenever White's knight from c3 moves, they might have problems on that diagonal.

rnbqk2r/pp4pp/2pbpn2/3p1p2/2PP4/2N1PNB1/.text:
White could choose to retreat here.

Capturing on g3 would only open up the h-file for their rook, but we have other plans.

Let's make use of our e4-square domination and jump there with the knight!

Now capturing on g3 might be an option, as it leaves us with the bishop pair.

rnbqk2r/pp4pp/2pbpn2/3pNp2/2PP1B2/2N1P3/.text:
White could choose to keep the dark-squared bishops on the board and play Ne5!

Capturing the knight with ...Bxe5 would only give White the active bishop on e5.

We can simply castle instead.

Although White has some space, they don't have any immediate threats.

rnbqkb1r/pp4pp/2p1pn2/3P1pB1/3P4/2N2N2/P.text:
Instead of developing with e3, White could choose to resolve matters in the center immediately with cxd5!

Capturing with the e-pawn maintains a nice pawn chain and keeps control of the b5-square.

rnbqkb1r/pp4pp/2p1pn2/3p1p2/2PP1B2/2N1PN.text:
White will usually continue in a natural manner, opening up the light-squared bishop...

And one of the key moves here is not to get passive with ...Be7, but rather challenge White's active bishop with ...Bd6!

We don't mind a trade here, although White has multiple options.

rnbqkb1r/pp4pp/2p1pn2/3p1pB1/2PP4/2N1PN2.text:
White's usual continuation is e3, opening the light-squared bishop.

It most often develops to the d3-square.

Activating the dark-squared bishop and unpinning the knight.

rnbqkb1r/pp4pp/2p2n2/3p1pB1/3P4/2N1PN2/P.text:
Now White can play e3, and we're back to the usual ideas.

Unpinning the knight and preparing ...Ne4 in the future.

We are ready to castle.

rnbqkb1r/ppp3pp/4pn2/3p1p2/2PP1B2/2N2N2/.text:
The most popular move by White, played 66% of the time, is Bf4.

Placing a lot of pawns on light squares means we've weakened the dark squares, so White takes control of those immediately!

I recommend ...c6 here, providing more protection to the center.

rnbqkb1r/ppp3pp/4pn2/3p1pB1/2PP4/2N2N2/P.text:
5.Bg5 is played about 12% of the time, but people love to pin the knight on f6, especially when it threatens to come to e4.

I simply recommend ...c6 here, strengthening the center and completing our pawn setup in the Stonewall Dutch.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/2N2N2/PP2.text:
This is the most common move in this position, played about 30% of the time.

We place a pawn in the center of the board!

Now we've got full control of the e4-square, and are planning to solidify the center with ...c6.

However, this weakens the e5-square, and White often takes advantage of that and places a piece there!

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5p2/2PP4/2N5/PP2PP.text:
You'll come across Nc3 71% of the time, it being the most popular move.

White develops the knight as well and contests some of the central squares.

As per usual, we'll focus on developing the kingside first.

Here, we strengthen the center and open up the dark-squared bishop.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White places two pawns in the center and grabs more space with c4.

We'll develop our knight and take more control of the e4-square.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the Stonewall Dutch! 

In this chapter, we'll take a look at the Stonewall setup for Black in the Dutch when White develops both knights to c3 and f3.

It is a very solid setup that is easy to play, usually consisting of pawns on the light squares such as f5, e6, d5 and c6.

Let's get started!

r1b1kb1r/pp4pp/2p5/3pP3/3Pp2q/4P1P1/PP2B.text:
White has to play g3 if they don't want to move their king.

Let's prevent them from castling!

r1b1kb1r/pp4pp/2p5/3pP3/3Pp3/4P1Pq/PP5P/.text: If they undevelop and attack our queen...

r1b1kb1r/pp4pp/2p5/3pPq2/3Pp3/4P1P1/PP5P.text:
We can simply move it back to the f5-square.

Next, you can simply finish development of the two bishops and castle.

White has only weakened their position and lost a tempo while we've developed the queen, and they still can't castle.

A great position for us!

r1bq1rk1/pp1N2pp/2pbpn2/3p1p2/2PP4/2NBP3.text:
Capturing the knight makes our life easy.

We'll recapture with the bishop.

r1bq1rk1/pp1n2pp/2pb1n2/3p1pB1/3P4/2N2NP.text:
We'll recapture with the e-pawn, as per usual. 

We can prepare ...Ne4 with ...Qe8, and if White offers a trade on f4, we can always slide our queen up to protect the bishop.

r1bq1rk1/pp1n2pp/2pb1n2/3pNp2/3P1P2/2NBP.text:
The most appealing move for White is to defend the knight with f4.

But there's also a very active move for one of our pieces!

r1bq1rk1/pp1n2pp/2pb4/3pNp2/3PnP2/2NBP3/.text:
Just like in Study 1, our knight arrives at e4 and is extremely active.

You should be familiar with positions like this one from the last study.

r1bq1rk1/pp1n2pp/2pbp3/3p1p2/2PPn3/1PNBP.text:
We will as well.

Our position is solid here and if allowed, we could go for something like ...g5 to strike on the kingside.

The center is closed off and we have a strong clamp on the e4-square, so a kingside attack could be possible.

r1bq1rk1/pp1n2pp/2pbp3/3pNp2/2PPNP2/3BP3.text:
If White decides to capture on e4...

This time we'll recapture with the d-pawn.

Capturing with the f-pawn is also fine, but it leaves White open for some f5-ideas in the future.

We attack the bishop now.

r1bq1rk1/pp1n2pp/2pbpn2/3P1pB1/3P4/2N2NP.text: White might try to resolve the central tension now.

r1bq1rk1/pp1n2pp/2pbpn2/3pNp2/2PP1P2/2NB.text:
If they choose to defend the knight with f4, they've chosen to play with space.

But that shouldn't demoralize us!

Let's continue with our main centralizing idea.

r1bq1rk1/pp1n2pp/3bp3/2p1Np2/2PPpP2/4P3/.text:
Here's another instance where ...c5 is a great positional move!

It challenges White's center and tries to destabilize their knight on e5.

If the c-file opens up in the future, we'll definitely want to play on it.

r1bqkb1r/pp1n2pp/2p2n2/3pNp2/3P1P2/2N1P3.text:
Should White decide to strengthen their knight with f4...

We can actually capture!

This line has more trades in the center than the others. 

But it goes to show that even the trades are beneficial for you and get you in a comfortable position!

r1bqkb1r/pp4pp/2p2n2/3pPp2/3P4/2N1P3/PP4.text:
Let's say White captures with the f-pawn.

What's the best square for your knight?

The active central e4-square!

r1bqkb1r/pp4pp/2p5/3pP3/3Pp3/4P3/PP2B1PP.text:
If White continues developing in a traditional manner, we can already start asking them some questions.

Check!

r1bqkb1r/pp4pp/2p5/3pPp2/3PN3/4P3/PP4PP/.text:
White captures.

Let's recapture with the f-pawn.

This way we get a strong pawn chain and open up our light-squared bishop.

r2q1rk1/pp1b2pp/2pbpn2/3p1p2/2PP4/2NBPP2.text:
An interesting approach is f3 by White, controlling the e4-square and disallowing ...Ne4 by us.

This is why they didn't play f4!

r4rk1/ppqb2pp/2pbpn2/3p1p2/2PP4/2NBPP2/P.text:
Let's not be discouraged, after all.

We can still develop our pieces and our position is very solid!

Here, the bishop and the queen together attack the h2-pawn.

rn1q1rk1/1p1b2pp/2pbp3/p2p1p2/1PPPn3/P1N.text:
And here comes b4.

We'll instigate matters ourselves and disallow White from expanding any further.

rn1q1rk1/2bb2pp/2p1p3/ppPp1p2/1P1Pn3/P1N.text:
We'll simply retreat to c7, keeping our position active.

Our pieces have a little less room to breathe than in the other lines, but we've successfully blocked White's advances on the queenside!

One of the plans you could go for is reactivating the d7-bishop on the kingside and developing your knight to d7.

rn1q1rk1/3b2pp/2pbp3/ppPp1p2/1P1Pn3/P1N2.text:
At this point, it's most logical for White to push the c5-pawn as it was under a lot of pressure.

This closes the position, though.

rnbq1rk1/1p4pp/2pbp3/p2p1p2/2PPn3/P1N2NP.text:
And make them play a3 to support the b4-push.

We usually develop the knight to d7 first, but in this instance we'll activate the bishop.

Once White plays b4, we are going to play ...b5 and block them from advancing!

The bishop provides more support to the b5-square.

rnbq1rk1/pp4pp/2pb1n2/3pNp2/3P4/2NBP3/PP.text:
Once they bring their knight to the center, that should signal something from us.

And that's to develop our queenside knight and challenge the knight on e5 immediately.

rnbq1rk1/pp4pp/2pbp3/3p1p2/2PPn3/2N2NP1/.text:
The GM-level response is Rb1 here.

White simply wants to play b4 and push on the queenside.

You might not encounter this as often in your games, but it is important to know as well.

Realizing what White wants to do, it's good to stop the immediate b4 by White...

rnbq1rk1/pp4pp/2pbpn2/3p1p2/2PP4/1PNBPN2.text:
A more defensive style of play is b3, defending the c4-pawn.

White wants to develop their bishop to b2, since they blocked it with the e-pawn.

We can still play ...Ne4.

Always be on the lookout for this move in the Stonewall Dutch!

rnbq1rk1/pp4pp/2pbpn2/3p1p2/2PP4/2N2NP1/.text:
8.Qc2 is the most common move in Grandmaster games, played about 60% of the time.

Having developed the bishop to g2, White wants to expand and play on the queenside.

This is a very specific but strong response by White to our Stonewall.

We'll continue with our usual ...Ne4.

rnbq1rk1/pp4pp/2pbpn2/3p1pB1/2PP4/2N2NP1.text:
The most natural-looking move is Bg5, developing the last minor piece and pinning the knight on f6.

White also takes advantage of our bishop not activating to e7 but rather to d6.

That's fine, we can also support our knight with the knight from d7!

rnbq1rk1/pp4pp/2pbpn2/3pNp2/2PP4/2NBP3/P.text:
At any point, White might choose to play Ne5.

Let's see how to battle it if they choose to centralize their knight in this position.

We'll, again, play ...Nbd7 to challenge the knight.

rnbqk2r/pp4pp/2pb1n2/3p1p2/3P4/2NBPN2/PP.text:
The less confrontational approach by White is to simply castle.

This is a very natural move you will encounter a lot.

We'll simply bring our king to safety as well.

rnbqk2r/pp4pp/2pbpn2/3p1p2/2PP4/2N2NP1/P.text:
White castles, having developed the kingside pieces...

And so do we.

From this moment on, White has three main options to continue.

rnbqk2r/pp4pp/2pbpn2/3p1p2/2PP4/2NBPN2/P.text:
Once White castles...

We can bring our king to safety as well.

rnbqkb1r/pp4pp/2p1pn2/3P1p2/3P4/2N1PN2/P.text:
If you remember the last study, you should know with which pawn to recapture in the center.

It's the e-pawn!

rnbqkb1r/pp4pp/2p1pn2/3p1p2/2PP4/2N2NP1/.text:
They'll probably follow up g3 with Bg2, ready to castle.

Let's activate our bishop to d6, from where it stares at the kingside.

rnbqkb1r/pp4pp/2p1pn2/3p1p2/2PP4/2NBPN2/.text:
Developing the bishop to the natural d3-square and eyeing the f5-pawn is played about 50% of the time.

We can simply continue developing, ready to castle.

White doesn't have a bishop on g5 for example so we can comfortably develop our bishop to d6.

rnbqkb1r/pp4pp/2p2n2/3p1p2/3P4/2NBPN2/PP.text:
White develops the bishop, ready to castle.

The bishop attacks the f5-pawn and there are lines where they add another attacker to it, as you'll see very soon.

Nothing is pinning our knight, so we don't need to get passive with ...Be7. Let's activate the bishop to d6.

rnbqkb1r/pp4pp/2p2n2/3pNp2/3P4/2N1P3/PP3.text:
Should White decide to shove the knight into the e5-square, do you know how to respond?

As per usual, we'll develop the queenside knight and create tension in the center.

rnbqkb1r/ppp3pp/4pn2/3p1p2/2PP4/2N1PN2/P.text:
5.e3 by White is only played about 4% of the time.

White opens up their light-squared bishop but blocks their bishop on c1.

This changes the position in the sense that we don't have to worry about an extra piece!

Our response is going to be ...c6, strengthening the center and completing the Stonewall setup.

rnbqkb1r/ppp3pp/4pn2/3p1p2/2PP4/2N2NP1/P.text:
Fifth move by White being g3 is played about 12% of the time, but it is certainly a variation that should be covered.

White wants to fianchetto their light-squared bishop and pressure the center from a different standpoint, without blocking the bishop on c1.

Our setup of pawns remains the same.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/2N2N2/PP2.text:
White replies by developing the other knight.

Let's strike in the center!

The ...d5-push is very typical in the Stonewall Dutch.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5p2/2PP4/2N5/PP2PP.text:
White replies with Nc3 most of the time.

Continuing development and opening up the dark-squared bishop.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
Two pawns in the center.

Let's develop our knight behind the f-pawn.

We've already got two pieces controlling the e4-square.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
In this study, we'll take a look at the lines that arise after 5.g3 or 5.e3 by White, and how to get our Stonewall setup in motion against those.

Let's dive right in!

r1b1k2r/pp1n2p1/2p2q1p/5p2/2P5/2P5/P3PPP.text:
Remember to recapture with the queen here, as it gets the queen off the d-file and attacks the c3-pawn.

We are down a pawn here, but White has weaknesses on the c-file and we've got the lead in development!

Next, we'll castle and develop the rest of the pieces.

r1b1k2r/pp1n2pp/2pqp3/3p1p2/2PPn3/2NBPN2.text:
Having developed all the pieces, White could develop the queen to c2, with the idea of Nd2 and f3.

Our knight on e4 is definitely the biggest problem in their position, so they will want to kick it out.

We'll castle out of danger.

r1b2rk1/pp1n2pp/2pqp3/3p1p2/2PPn3/2NBP3/.text:
Once Nd2 is played, I have an interesting idea to offer.

You might be able to use it very often in the Dutch, as it takes advantage of the f-pawn being on f5.

Or rook is coming to h6, and together with the queen on d6 will attack the h2-square.

Our queen already being on d6 was made possible by White's early Bf4 and the trade of bishops on d6.

r1b2rk1/pp1nq1pp/2p1p3/3p1p2/2PPP3/2NB1P.text:
The most aggressive approach by White is to play e4 here, proving their point of the Nge2 and f3 setup.

Now there's a lot of tension in the center!

I recommend capturing with the d-pawn here and keeping the f-file closed.

r1b2rk1/pp1nq1pp/2p1p3/5p2/2PPP3/2NB4/PP.text: White will recapture with the f-pawn...

r1b2rk1/pp1nq1pp/2p5/4pp2/2PPP3/2NB4/PP4.text:
And try to remember the ...e5-push here!

If you remember the last chapter, this was one of the key pushes we wanted to achieve in some lines.

Here, it's possible and challenges the d4-pawn.

It's bad for White to capture on e5 and let us recapture with the knight.

r1b3k1/pp1n2pp/2pqp2r/3p1p2/2PPn3/2NBPP2.text:
We can still go for the ...Rh6 idea!

The computer actually recommends f4 for White here to block our queen, which would leave our knight on e4.

White could theoretically also capture the knight, but they would have to defend after ...Qxh2+ and ...fxe4 with a lot of space for us to attack.

r1b3k1/pp1n2pp/2pqpr2/3p1p2/2PPn3/2NBPP2.text: Even if White attacks our knight...

rnb1k2r/pp4pp/2pqp3/3p1p2/2PPn3/2NBPN2/P.text:
White will probably castle here.

The second standard move in our setup for the middlegame.

rnb1k2r/pp4pp/2pqpn2/3p1p2/2PP4/2NBPN2/P.text:
Once White plays Nf3, we've reached a position similar to ones you've seen in Chapter 5.

Our plans are similar as well: get the knights to the e4- and d7-squares and castle.

And that's what we'll start doing.

rnb2rk1/pp2q1pp/2p1p3/3p1p2/2PP4/2NBPP2/.text:
Recapturing with the knight is more logical than doubling the c-pawns and one of the other ideas of Nge2.

A standard developing move by us, controlling the e5-square.

Pushing ...e5 now is definitely on the cards.

rnb2rk1/pp2q1pp/2p1p3/3p1p2/2PPn3/2NBPP2.text:
White will put the f3-plan into motion.

Let's capture on c3.

This is more efficient than retreating and giving White the momentum.

rnbq1rk1/pp1p2pp/2p1pn2/6B1/1bPP4/2NB4/P.text: Once White develops the light-squared bishop...

rnbq1rk1/pp1p2pp/4pn2/2p3B1/1bPP4/2NB4/P.text:
We'll do just that.

White's best response is to avoid the central tension with d5, but that's okay.

We'll remove the c3-knight, simply capture on d5 and play ...d6 to keep developing.

If White doesn't push d5, we might even push it at some point.

rnbq1rk1/pp2B1pp/2p1p3/3p1p2/2PPn3/2NBP3.text:
White will most likely capture on e7.

We'll recapture and activate the queen.

rnbq1rk1/pp2b1pp/2p1pn2/3p1pB1/2PP4/2NBP.text:
And so will they.

Now that we've reached the middlegame, and your knight is not pinned anymore, what's the first move that should come to mind?

Centralizing the knight on e4!

This also initiates tension between the dark-squared bishops.

rnbqk2r/pp1P2p1/2p2n1p/5pB1/2P5/2P5/P3PP.text:
In most cases, you'll encounter White capturing again, as it comes with check and wins a pawn for them.

But that's okay! We'll recapture and continue to develop.

White's bishop is still under attack.

rnbqk2r/pp1p2pp/2p1Pn2/5pB1/1bP5/2N5/PP2.text:
That's why White will probably capture themselves.

Capturing on e6 definitely creates more problems for us than capturing on c6, as dxc6 would just let us develop with ...Nxc6.

Let's capture on c3 and make White double their pawns.

That's why we played ...Bb4 after all.

rnbqk2r/pp1p2pp/2p1Pn2/5pB1/2P5/2P5/P3PP.text:
They'll capture...

And I actually don't recommend recapturing on e6 right away, as White could trade queens in that instance.

Instead, we attack the bishop on g5.

rnbqk2r/pp1p2pp/2p1pn2/6B1/1bPP4/2N5/PP3.text:
The better option for them is definitely to keep the castling rights.

But now there is no additional pressure on our knight on f6!

We can simply castle, with an active rook.

We are looking to play ...c5 in this position to challenge White's d4-pawn.

rnbqk2r/pp2b1pp/2p1pn2/3p1pB1/2PP4/2NBP3.text:
White will continue with their plan, also ready to castle.

We'll bring the king to safety...

rnbqk2r/pp4pp/2pBpn2/3p1p2/2PP4/2NBP3/PP.text:
So they will most likely capture on d6.

Of course, we recapture and activate the queen.

rnbqkb1r/pp1p2pp/2p1pn2/3P1pB1/2P5/2N5/P.text:
White could decide to take advantage of no pawn being on d5 and push d5 themselves, although it happens very rarely.

I recommend pinning their knight here with ...Bb4.

This basically removes a defender of the d5-square and develops our bishop at the same time.

Now capturing on d5 becomes possible.

rnbqkb1r/pp1p2pp/2p1pn2/5pB1/2PP4/2N1P3/.text:
The more passive but definitely the most common approach, played about 40% of the time, is e3.

White simply opens up the light-squared bishop.

They've given us room to push the d-pawn, so let's push it!

Now we've achieved our Stonewall setup with the pawns on the light squares.

rnbqkb1r/pp1p2pp/2p1pn2/5pB1/2PPP3/2N5/P.text:
Another way White can take advantage of our pinned knight is e4. It happens almost a quarter of the time.

They've got three pawns in the center now, but there's nothing to fear.

Let's capture on e4, removing one of the pawns immediately. That's why we played ...f5 on move 1!

rnbqkb1r/pp1p2pp/2p1pn2/6B1/2PPN3/8/PP3P.text:
White will definitely recapture and put more pressure on our pinned knight.

Remember this next move!

This check is more useful to give than the passive ...Be7.

We force White to either move their king or to retreat the knight!

rnbqkb1r/pp4pp/2p1pn2/3p1p2/2PP1B2/2NBP3.text:
Developing the bishop.

We'll do the same, creating tension between the dark-squared bishops.

White shouldn't let us capture on f4, as that would disrupt their pawn chain...

rnbqkb1r/pp4pp/2p1pn2/3p1pB1/2PP4/2NBP3/.text:
In order to avoid the 2 Knights setup, White will first develop the light-squared bishop.

Their plan is going to consist of activating the knight to e2 and playing f3 once we play ...Ne4.

They might follow it up with e4 as well.

Let's unpin our knight for now and prepare castling.

rnbqkb1r/ppp3pp/4pn2/3p1p2/2PP1B2/2N1P3/.text:
White will most likely continue in a traditional manner, opening up the light-squared bishop.

And we'll complete the Stonewall Setup!

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP1B2/2N5/PP2.text:
White playing Bf4 on move 4 is not played as often as Bg5 (only 7% of the time), but you might definitely come across this line.

White hasn't challenged us in any way, so we can continue with our setup.

And we will, placing a pawn in the center.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5pB1/2PP4/2N5/PP2P.text:
Let's see how to play the Stonewall if White decides to pin our knight immediately with Bg5, which is played 28% of the time.

The problem is, ...d5 right away is impossible because White could capture on d5 and then capture on f6.

So what do we do? Although is looks ugly, we have to play ...c6 to prepare ...d5.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5p2/2PP4/2N5/PP2PP.text:
White activates the knight on the natural c3-square and takes control of some of the key central squares.

Remember to create this nice pawn chain in the opening.

This also helps your dark-squared bishop develop!

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White places two pawns in the center of the board, grabbing more space.

The usual continuation.

Behind the pawn comes the knight!

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
In this study, we'll take a look at how to play the Stonewall against White's 3.Nc3 and 4.Bg5 or 4.Bf4.

White doesn't activate the kingside knight to f3 but rather to e2 in many cases and leaves options open for f3 or f4 from the get-go.

Let's take a look!

rnb2rk1/pp2q1pp/2pbpn2/3p1p2/2PP1N2/2NBP.text:
We can activate the queen and add more protection to the e6-pawn.

Next, we'll develop the rest of the pieces and look to play ...e5.

rnbq1rk1/pp4pp/2pb1n2/3p1p2/3P4/2N2NP1/P.text: And so do we, with the standard ideas to follow.

rnbq1rk1/pp4pp/2pbpn2/3p1p2/2PP1B2/2N3PN.text:
White castles as well.

Next, we'll develop the queenside pieces.

Just make sure you don't play ...Nbd7 before you protect your d6-bishop and hang it!

So we'll simply castle and let them capture if they want to.

Next, we'll develop the queenside pieces.

Just make sure you don't play ...Nbd7 before you protect your d6-bishop!

rnbq1rk1/pp5p/2pb1np1/3p1p2/3P4/2NBP3/PP.text:
And so do we.

You already know what the next moves are.

Centralizing the knight, developing the other one and simply activating the rest of the pieces.

rnbqk2r/pp4pp/2pbpn2/3p1p2/2PP1B2/2N3PN/.text:
White develops the bishop to f4.

Capturing on f4 would only play into their hands and activate their knight...

rnbqk2r/pp4pp/2pbpn2/3p1p2/2PP1N2/2NBP3/.text:
The knight on f4 is nothing scary, as our center is sufficiently defended.

If anything, the knight on f4 is just an additional target if we play ...e5!

Let's simply castle.

rnbqk2r/pp4pp/2pbpn2/3p1p2/2PP4/2NBP3/PP.text:
Just develop the bishop, as you would under different circumstances as well.

You already know how to play this position, and you have the benefit of White's bishop being blocked in!

rnbqkb1r/pp4pp/2p1pn2/3p1p2/2PP4/2N3PN/P.text:
An interesting developing move is Nh3, not blocking the bishop.

The idea is to play Bf4 and recapture with the knight if the trade on f4 happens.

We'll anticipate that and develop our bishop to d6.

rnbqkb1r/pp4pp/2p1pn2/3p1p2/2PP4/2NBP2N/.text:
Instead of developing the knight to e2, White might choose to activate it via the h3-square.

Their plan would be to place the knight on f4.

Our setup shouldn't change; we'll develop the bishop to the most active square.

rnbqkb1r/pp4pp/2p1pn2/3p1p2/2PP4/2NBP3/P.text: White might go for the Nge2 approach we've seen in the previous study.

rnbqkb1r/pp4pp/2p2n2/3p1p2/3P4/2N2NP1/PP.text:
Let's say White activates the knight to f3 instead of h3 in this variation.

This should signal you that ...Ne4 is very much on the cards, as the f-pawn can't move.

First, let's complete kingside development and get ready to castle.

rnbqkb1r/pp4pp/2p2n2/3p1p2/3P4/2NBP3/PPQ.text:
Definitely an aggressive approach, attacking the f5-pawn with one more piece.

If you remember from the last chapter, one of the ways we deal with this is simply ...g6, defending the pawn.

We aren't afraid of the dark squares being weak, as White's dark-squared bishop is out of bounds for the moment!

rnbqkb1r/pp5p/2p2np1/3p1p2/3P4/2NBP3/PPQ.text:
White plays Nge2, looking to potentially move the f-pawn in the future.

Let's finish kingside development.

We'll castle next.

rnbqkb1r/ppp3pp/4pn2/3P1p2/3P4/2N1P3/PP3.text:
White opting for the center exchange before we play ...c6 is okay as well.

We'll just recapture with the e-pawn, and still play ...c6 to support it on the next move.

If anything, this helps us develop with more space!

rnbqkb1r/ppp3pp/4pn2/3P1p2/3P4/2N3P1/PP2.text:
White could also capture in the center in this position.

We'll simply recapture, with the same ideas of ...c6.

rnbqkb1r/ppp3pp/4pn2/3p1p2/2PP4/2N3P1/PP.text:
Once White develops the bishop...

We'll complete the Stonewall!

Their bishop isn't as useful as they might have thought it would be.

rnbqkb1r/ppp3pp/4pn2/3p1p2/2PP4/2NBP3/PP.text:
After playing e3, White usually follows through with Bd3, activating the light-squared bishop.

A position we've already seen in previous studies.

Our moves don't change; we'll go for the Stonewall setup.

rnbqkb1r/ppp3pp/5n2/3p1p2/3P4/2N3P1/PP2P.text:
Completing the fianchetto.

But running right into a wall of pawns on light squares.

rnbqkb1r/ppp3pp/5n2/3p1p2/3P4/2NBP3/PP3P.text:
A natural developing move, targeting the defended f5-pawn.

Let's strengthen the center and take away the b5-square from White.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/2N1P3/PP3.text:
4.e3 is played about 22% of the time in this position, in high-level games.

The biggest downside is that the bishop on c1 is restricted from developing!

We'll continue with ...d5, as we are allowed to.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/2N3P1/PP2.text:
Going for the fianchetto with g3 is played 17% of the time by White.

They want to take control of the long diagonal rather than developing the light-squared bishop to d3.

We'll strike in the center.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5p2/2PP4/2N5/PP2PP.text:
White will most often develop the queenside knight here.

And we'll build a nice pawn chain while opening up the dark-squared bishop.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
The standard two pawns in the center by White.

Let's develop a piece and take more control of the e4-square.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
In this study, we'll take a look at some little less common setups by White, in 4.e3 and 4.g3.

By playing these moves, White either blocks in their dark-squared bishop or goes for the light-squared bishop fianchetto.

Let's learn how to play against these approaches!

r1b1k1r1/pp1nq2p/2pbpn2/3pNpp1/2PP4/1P4P.text:
The position is somewhat closed in the center and on the queenside, so our king is safe for now.

The attack is more important! We'll place the rook on g8 to support the g-pawn and advance the h-pawn.

Our goal is to get it to h4 and undermine White's structure around the king.

r1b1k2r/pp1nq1pp/2pbpn2/3pNp2/2PP4/1P4P1.text:
...Which White conveniently stops with Bb2.

However, their knight is stuck in the center and isn't controlling the g5-square anymore.

Which allows us to move forward with ...g5!

The idea is simply to create a pawn storm and attack the king.

r1b1k2r/pp1nq2p/2pbpn2/3pNpp1/2PP4/1P4P1.text:
White won't be able to do much but develop here.

Their pieces are activated, but can't do much in terms of defending against our pawn storm, which was initiated by White relinquishing control of g5.

Any time a piece moves, look for which squares it stops controlling!

r1b2rk1/4q1pp/n1pbpn2/p2p1p2/1pPP4/PP3NP.text:
Well, we won't.

We'll simply add protection to the b4-pawn.

White's position is very cramped and they are lacking space on the queenside.

r1b2rk1/pp1nq1pp/2pbp3/3p1p2/2PPn3/1PN2N.text:
But that's fine, as we'll develop to d7.

Now White can't even play Ne5.

In the future, we'll play on the queenside with moves such as ...b6, ...a5 and ...Ba6 to target the c4-pawn.

Since White doesn't have Ne5, our bishop doesn't need to defend from b7 and is more active on a6.

r1bq1rk1/pp1n2pp/2p1p3/3p1p2/2PPnP2/2N1P.text:
Let's take advantage of our control of the e4-square and centralize the knight.

We've got various ideas here, such as the standard rook lift to f6, simply developing our queen to e7 or expanding on the queenside with ...a5.

r1bq1rk1/pp1n2pp/2p1pn2/3p1p2/2PP1P2/2N1.text:
White continues developing as well, and we deploy the known improving move with the knight.

You probably know what it is.

r1bqk2r/pp1n2pp/2pbpn2/3p1pB1/2PP4/5NP1/.text:
We'll simply support the knight, with plans of ...h6 and ...O-O.

The good thing about ...h6 is that White can't play Bh4 because of ...g5.

rn3rk1/pb2q1pp/1ppbpn2/3pNp2/2PP4/1P4P1/.text:
But we can defend it with the bishop.

Next, we'll get our knight to d7 to challenge White's knight and place the rook on the c-file to support the c-pawns and occupy the file if it opens up.

rnb1k2r/1p2q1pp/2pbpn2/p2p1p2/P1PP4/BP3N.text:
White puts their plan in motion and plays Ba3.

Let's trade.

rnb1k2r/pp2q1pp/2pbpn2/3p1p2/2PP4/1P3NP1.text:
Realizing they can't go Ba3, White will usually activate the bishop to b2 in this position, having played b3.

Their idea, as mentioned, is to play Qc1 and add more support to the a3-square.

We've completed kingside development, so let's castle out of the way.

rnb1k2r/pp2q1pp/2pbpn2/3p1p2/P1PP4/1P3NP.text:
The idea behind a4 is that the rook now covers the a3-square as well!

This reinitiates the threat of Ba3 and there isn't much we can do to stop it.

The bad thing about a4 is that White's queenside is now overextended, with the weak b3-pawn.

We'll stop their advancement right away and play against those weaknesses later.

rnb1k2r/pp2q1pp/2pbpn2/3pNp2/2PP4/1P4P1/.text:
Instead of immediately following up with Bb2, there is always the idea of Ne5.

In the Stonewall, White will most often have control of the e5-square, so we need to be prepared for Ne5 to arrive at any moment!

We'll challenge the knight right away by developing a piece.

Right now, we are threatening to capture on e5 and win a pawn...

rnb2rk1/1p2q1pp/2p1pn2/p2p1p2/P1PP4/NP3N.text:
We'll just castle.

Our position is still comfortable with nothing to be afraid of.

rnb2rk1/4q1pp/2pbpn2/p2p1p2/1pPP4/PP3NP1.text: If White plays a3, aiming for Bxa3 if we capture...

rnb2rk1/p1b1q1pp/2p1pn2/1pPpNp2/3P4/1P4P.text:
White will probably have to switch up their gameplan and go for something like Ne5, centralizing the knight.

We'll still go for our ...b4 idea and completely restrict White's bishop on b2.

rnb2rk1/p1b1q1pp/2p1pn2/2PpNp2/3P4/pP4P1.text:
It's okay to capture on a3.

We still have a comfortable position.

If White recaptures with the bishop, it will only be staring at its own pawn on c5.

rnb2rk1/p3q1pp/1p1bpn2/3pNp2/3P4/1P4P1/P.text:
In this case, we can actually recapture with our c-pawn. 

This is one of those few rare cases in which we can do this. 

If White plays Nc3, we can go ...Ba6 to develop the bishop to a great diagonal, but also to cover the b5-square. 

We'll also put a rook on c8 and start making use of that open c-file.

rnb2rk1/p3q1pp/1ppbpn2/3pNp2/2PP4/1P4P1/.text: White might centralize the knight and attack the weakened c6-pawn.

rnb2rk1/p3q1pp/2pbpn2/1p1p1p2/2PP4/BP3NP.text:
If White disregards our last move and still goes for Ba3...

We'll shut down any ideas of White accomplishing their mission of trading the dark-squared bishops!

rnb2rk1/p3q1pp/2pbpn2/1pPp1p2/3P4/1P3NP1.text:
Avoiding any of the pawn trades and closing down the center with tempo is another way of playing White might opt for.

That's okay, going for c5 means Ba3 isn't nearly as potent anymore.

rnb2rk1/p3q1pp/2pbpn2/3p1p2/1pPP4/1P3NP1.text:
Going back to b2 is the only sensible move.

Having expanded on the queenside, let's support the b-pawn with ...a5.

rnb2rk1/p3q1pp/3bpn2/1p1p1p2/3P4/1P3NP1/.text:
We'll simply recapture, with the same idea.

We'll develop in a standard manner with ...Bb7 and ...Nd7.

rnb2rk1/pp2q1pp/2pbp3/3p1p2/2PPn3/1PN2NP.text: White might go for the Qc2-approach...

rnb2rk1/pp2q1pp/2pbpn2/3p1p2/2PP4/1P3NP1.text:
Something like Nbd2 is more natural, simply developing the knight and playing traditionally.

This doesn't cause us any problems, so we'll simply continue developing ourselves.

The main idea for our light-squared bishop is ...b6 and ...Bb7.

Following the main idea, White will play Qc1 and go for Ba3 on the next move.

However, I don't necessarily think you will face this move the most in your games.

We'll advance the b-pawn and put even more pressure on c4!

Another idea is to counter Ba3 with b4.

rnb2rk1/pp2q1pp/2pbpn2/3p1p2/2PP4/1PN2NP.text:
Another natural move is Nc3, developing but placing the knight in front of the bishop.

In this case, we can challenge the knight right away.

Let's play ...Ne4 and centralize a piece.

rnb2rk1/pp2q1pp/2pbpn2/3pNp2/2PP4/1P4P1/.text:
Going for Ne5 here might also happen.

Before we challenge the knight, let's make sure we develop our light-squared bishop to b7.

rnbq1rk1/pp4pp/2p1pn2/3p1p2/2PP1P2/4PN2/.text:
White now has a cluster of dark-squared pawns, keeping their structure together.

We haven't faced any threats yet, however, and should simply keep developing.

The usual way, of course.

Most often in the Stonewall will the queenside knight get out before the light-squared bishop.

rnbqk2r/pp4pp/2p1pn2/3p1p2/2PP1P2/5N2/PP.text:
White captures, doubling their pawns on the f-file.

However, they do get excellent control of the central dark squares to replace their bishop, and the grip on e5.

Let's simply get the king out of any potential danger.

rnbqk2r/pp4pp/2pbpn2/3p1p2/2PP1B2/5NP1/P.text:
Another idea White could definitely go for is Bf4, the more direct approach of trying to trade bishops.

This lets us capture on f4 and ruin their kingside pawn structure, though.

That is why most players who play the Nf3 setups against the Stonewall Dutch go for the b3-Ba3 ideas.

rnbqk2r/pp4pp/2pbpn2/3p1p2/2PP4/1P3NP1/P.text:
7. b3 is the main line at top level and the second most popular move at amateur level. 

The idea is very often playing Ba3, or Bb2-Qc1-Ba3, in order to trade the dark-squared bishops.

Anticipating that, we'll play ...Qe7.

Rather than just mindlessly castling, we see White's plan and play against it!

rnbqk2r/pp4pp/2pbpn2/3p1p2/2PP4/2N2NP1/P.text: This move-order transposes to what we've already seen, the 2 Knights setup with White playing g3.

rnbqk2r/pp4pp/2pbpn2/3p1pB1/2PP4/5NP1/PP.text:
If White goes for Bg5, pinning the knight, don't be scared.

You've already come across positions like this one.

rnbqkb1r/pp4pp/2p1pn2/3p1p2/2PP4/5NP1/PP.text:
When choosing to play setups like these, White very often quickly activates the kingside and castles.

It's time for us to catch up in development.

The d6-square is most active for our bishop.

rnbqkb1r/ppp3pp/4pn2/3p1p2/2PP4/5NP1/PP2.text:
White develops the bishop...

And we'll complete our configuration.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/5NP1/PP2P.text:
In this study, we'll cover 4.g3 by White, being the most popular move played 62% of the time.

White wants to fianchetto in Catalan style.

As we have before, let's strike in the center.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5p2/2PP4/5N2/PP2PP.text:
Nf3 is the third most popular move, being played 17% of the time, but the positions often transpose into the 2 Knights setups.

However, if White knows where they're going with this, it's crucial for you to know how to play against the Nf3 setups!

We create a pawn chain and open up the dark-squared bishop. We'll have a pawn coming to d5 next!

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White takes advantage of being first to move and places two pawns in the center...

...And we'll build behind the f-pawn to activate our first piece.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
In this chapter, we'll take a look at how to play our already known Stonewall Dutch if White decides to go for various Nf3 setups.

Let's dive right in!

rnbqk2r/pp2b1pp/2p1p3/3p1pB1/2PPn3/3BPN2.text:
But we're just in time to block their attack!

You should be familiar with this position.

rnbqk2r/pp2b1pp/2p1pn2/3p1pB1/2PP4/3BPN2.text: White's idea might be Qc2, trying to possibly capture in the center and weaken our f5-pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pp4pp/2p1pn2/3p1p2/2PP1B2/4PN2/.text:
And after ...c6, we've had the exact same position with the knight on c3 already.

The knight being on f3 shouldn't change anything, and you know how to fight against Ne5.

White will play Nc3 and transpose very often anyway.

rnbqkb1r/pp4pp/2p1pn2/3p1pB1/2PP4/3BPN2/.text:
White will probably develop to d3...

And I recommend unpinning the knight with ...Be7 here.

Although it looks a little bit passive, it's a sound defensive move.

The idea is to free the knight to jump to e4 on the next move.

rnbqkb1r/ppp3pp/4pn2/3p1p2/2PP1B2/4PN2/P.text: White will probably play e3, as in the main line...

rnbqkb1r/ppp3pp/4pn2/3p1pB1/2PP4/4PN2/PP.text:
Opening up the light-squared bishop.

Let's complete the Stonewall setup of pawns.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP1B2/5N2/PP2.text:
Going for Bf4 instead of Bg5 simply cannot avoid a transposition into something we've already covered.

It's played only 2% of the time.

Let's go for our usual ...d5 idea.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5pB1/2PP4/5N2/PP2P.text:
Placing the bishop to g5 pins our knight on f6 immediately, played only 1% of the time.

But it's something we've already seen before.

We'll still play ...d5, grabbing space in the center.

If White captures on d5, we'll gladly recapture with the e-pawn.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5p2/2PP4/5N2/PP2PP.text:
White will go for the Nf3 setup with 3.Nf3...

And we'll prepare ...d5.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
Two pawns in the center.

We'll develop the knight to f6.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
In Study 2, we'll quickly take a look at Bg5 or Bf4 on move 4 by White.

It will be a very short study, as both the moves have already been seen in previous chapters and the positions that arise are very similar.

Again, there are transpositions very often.

r1b2rk1/pp1nq1pp/2p1pn2/3p1p2/2PP4/1P1BP.text:
We'll activate the queenside knight.

Our ideas for developing the c8-bishop are ...b6 and ...Ba6 to target c4.

On the kingside and in the center, we'll restrict White even more with ...Ne4 and then often times push ...g5 to start an attack!

We can follow it up by getting the rook into the game via ...Rf6 and ...Rh6.

r1b2rk1/pp1nq1pp/2pb4/3p1p2/3Pn3/1P1BPN2.text:
And we'll castle.

As we've shown, White really should stick to the traditional Nc3 setup.

They've achieved nothing developing this way.

r1bqk2r/pp1n2pp/2pb4/3p1p2/3Pn3/1P1BPN2/.text:
Again, the most common developing path for the dark-squared bishop is b3 and Bb2/Ba3 when White plays e3.

Before castling, let's add support to the a3-square while developing the queen, just in case.

r2q1rk1/ppp3pp/2npbn2/5p2/2P5/2N1PN2/PP1.text:
...And we'll keep developing as well.

We've successfully fought against White's aggression on d5!

rn1q1rk1/ppp3pp/3pbn2/5p2/2P5/2N1PN2/PP1.text: White defends by opening up the light-squared bishop...

rn1qk2r/ppp3pp/3pbn2/5p2/2P5/2P2N2/P3PPP.text: Now our bishop is activated, with pressure on the c4-pawn.

rnbq1rk1/pp1p2pp/2p1pn2/3P1p2/2P5/4PN2/P.text:
We add another pawn and force the trade.

This trade will bring our pieces to life!

rnbq1rk1/pp1pb1pp/2P1pn2/5p2/2P5/P3PN2/1.text:
Capturing on c6 splits our central pawns.

We'll recapture with the d-pawn in both instances here, against dxc6 and dxe6 too.

Recapturing with the d-pawn opens up our queen and controls the d3-square so that White's bishop can't develop there.

rnbq1rk1/pp2b1pp/2p1pn2/5p2/2P5/P3PN2/1P.text: So it has to develop to a more passive square like e2.

rnbq1rk1/pp2b1pp/4pn2/2p2p2/2P5/P3PN2/1P.text:
Now we'll take the opportunity and play ...c5.

Remembering this move is useful for development, as we want to activate the knight to c6 and not block our queen on d8.

To expand in the center, we'll try to play ...e5, as nothing is stopping us!

rnbq1rk1/pp4pp/2p1pn2/3p1p2/2PP4/NP1BPN2.text:
It has to come to a3.

Which allows us to activate the queen with tempo.

Clumsy play by White.

rnbq1rk1/pp4pp/2pbpn2/3p1p2/2PP4/BP1BPN2.text:
They'll do just that.

I recommend capturing here and forcing White to activate the knight to an awkward square.

rnbq1rk1/ppp3pp/3pPn2/5p2/2P5/2N2N2/PP1Q.text:
They will probably realize our plan and capture now.

Now it's even less of a problem, though...

As it simply activates our bishop with an attack on the c4-pawn.

We'll develop with ...Nc6 next.

rnbq1rk1/ppp3pp/4pn2/5p2/2P5/5N2/PP1NPPP.text:
There's no problem.

Again, we'll look to expand with ...e5 and develop our knight with ...Nc6.

rnbq1rk1/pppp2pp/4pn2/3P1p2/1bP5/P4N2/1P.text:
Once White attacks our bishop...

We'll retreat to e7, as retreating to d6 would block our d6-pawn.

rnbq1rk1/pppp2pp/4pn2/3P1p2/2P5/2N2N2/PP.text:
White might play Nc3 here to keep developing.

Let's go for ...d6, with the idea of ...e5.

If White doesn't want to capture, we'll play our own way!

rnbq1rk1/pppp2pp/4pn2/3P1p2/2P5/4PN2/PP1.text:
Going for a more passive, but definitely solid approach is e3, opening up the light-squared bishop.

Do you remember what to do if White delays capturing on e6?

rnbq1rk1/ppppb1pp/4pn2/3P1p2/2P5/P3PN2/1.text:
If White doesn't capture on e6 and opens up the light-squared bishop instead...

We'll put more pressure on the d5-pawn!

Now White has to make a decision.

rnbqk2r/2p3pp/4pn2/P1bp1p2/8/4PN2/P4PPP/.text:
We'll activate our bishop as well.

As you can see, White's queenside pawn structure is completely ruined!

The a5-pawn is just waiting to get captured.

rnbqk2r/pp4pp/2pb1n2/3p1p2/3P4/3BPN2/PPQ.text:
When they play Qc2...

We'll go for the same idea as in the previous chapters, blocking the attack.

rnbqk2r/pp4pp/2pb4/3p1p2/3Pn3/3BPN2/PPQN.text:
White might challenge our knight, but it is sufficiently defended.

Let's just keep developing, with the idea of ...Ndf6.

We are also preventing Ne5 for the moment.

rnbqk2r/pp4pp/2pbpn2/3p1p2/2PP4/1P1BPN2/.text:
Having blocked in their dark-squared bishop, White will most likely develop via b3 and Ba3 to offer a trade of bishops.

Once we castle...

rnbqk2r/pp4pp/2pbpn2/3p1p2/2PP4/4PN2/PP2.text:
Let's activate the bishop to d6.

Our gameplans stay the same here, and any setup White can now play is worse than the one with the bishop on d3.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/3P1p2/1bP5/2N2N2/PP.text:
Another move here is Nc3, blocking with the knight on c3.

This might not be the best approach, though, because of our next move.

We'll capture on c3 and double White's c-pawns.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/3P1p2/1bP5/5N2/PP1B.text:
The most confrontational approach is to block with the bishop and initiate the tension.

We'll take, as retreating would be too passive.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/3P1p2/1bP5/5N2/PP1N.text:
Avoiding doubling the c-pawns, White could block with the knight on d2.

Let's castle out of the way.

We don't need to capture on d2 in this line and help White develop.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/3P1p2/2P5/2P2N2/P3P.text:
Their structure is definitely weakened.

We'll deal with White's central pressure by playing ...d6.

This enables our bishop to recapture if White decides to capture on e6.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/3P1p2/2P5/5N2/PP1NP.text:
Recapturing with the knight develops it at the same time.

However, it blocks the queen on d1 and lets us recapture on e6 without having to worry about trading queens.

We'll castle.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/3P1p2/2P5/5N2/PP1QP.text:
If White recaptures with the queen, they preserve the pressure on the d-file.

We'll castle out of the way.

We don't mind a queen trade if White captures on e6 now, as we've already castled and can recapture with the rook.

rnbqkb1r/2p3pp/1p2pn2/3p1p2/3P4/4PN2/PP3.text:
We'll simply recapture with the a-pawn and open up our rook.

Next, we'll activate the bishop and castle.

Playing this way, White has only helped us develop!

rnbqkb1r/2p3pp/1p2pn2/P1Pp1p2/3P4/4PN2/P.text:
So they pretty much have to capture and loosen the defence of c5.

This works immensely in our favor!

We'll capture on c5 and leave the a5-pawn weak.

rnbqkb1r/p1p3pp/1P2pn2/3p1p2/3P4/4PN2/PP.text: If White captures on b6, they've accomplished nothing by pushing the c-pawn forward.

rnbqkb1r/p1p3pp/1p2pn2/2Pp1p2/1P1P4/4PN2.text:
If White defends with b4, we have more to come at them with.

Let's attack the b4-pawn as well!

White can't play a3, because of the a-file opening, and can't play c3 because the c-pawn is on c5...

rnbqkb1r/pp4pp/2p1pn2/3p1p2/2PP4/3BPN2/P.text:
If White castles...

We'll develop our bishop to the most active square.

rnbqkb1r/pp4pp/2p2n2/3p1p2/3P4/3BPN2/PP3.text:
White has developed the kingside, so they castle.

We don't have to do anything about the f5-pawn until White attacks it.

rnbqkb1r/ppp3pp/4pn2/2Pp1p2/3P4/4PN2/PP3.text:
Going for c5 is very ambitious, trying to grab space and close down the center.

Let's punish White for this way of playing.

We'll challenge their structure immediately.

rnbqkb1r/ppp3pp/4pn2/3P1p2/3P4/4PN2/PP3P.text:
A move you might face often is capturing in the center immediately.

We have an easy decision which pawn to recapture with.

rnbqkb1r/ppp3pp/4pn2/3p1p2/2PP4/3BPN2/PP.text:
Another approach instead of c5 is developing the bishop to d3.

This is nothing special and something we've already seen.

We'll continue with our usual ...c6.

rnbqkb1r/ppp3pp/4pn2/3p1p2/2PP4/4PN2/PP2.text:
Developing the bishop to e2 is simply a more passive and an inferior approach to Bd3.

Our play will stay the same, and White won't have the added pressure with the bishop to d3.

We'll complete the Stonewall.

rnbqkb1r/ppp3pp/5n2/3p1p2/3P4/3BPN2/PP3P.text:
The rest of the moves in this line are pretty standard, and go to show that delaying Nc3 wouldn't help White whatsoever.

Here, they attack the f5-pawn.

The usual idea is to play Qc2 and add another attacker to it.

Let's reinforce the center.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/3P1p2/2P5/5N2/PP2P.text:
Pushing d5 right away is played only 1% of the time, but it could definitely become dangerous if we don't know what to do.

When White committs early, it's often smart to develop and castle as quickly as possible.

Here, we activate the bishop with tempo, giving a check.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/4PN2/PP3P.text:
Pushing e3 on move 4 is played only 5% of the time.

The obvious downside is that the bishop on c1 is blocked in!

Let's see how much our setup should change depending on what White plays.

For now, we'll still go ...d5.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5p2/2PP4/5N2/PP2PP.text:
White chooses to play Nf3.

We'll prepare the Stonewall with ...e6.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White responds with c4, grabbing more central space.

Let's activate the knight and control the e4-square with another piece.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
It's time to take a look at some of White's "strange" approaches, such as 4.e3 or 4.d5.

These moves don't occur very often but can certainly catch us by surprise if we are not theoretically prepared!
